newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean stocks jump as strike fears ease.
newsitem.headline: South Korean stocks jump as strike fears ease.

text.p: South Korean stocks rallied on Tuesday morning after a weak response by workers to trade union calls for an all-out strike and signs of improving market fundamentals, brokers said.
The composite index soared 2.84 percent, or 18.71 points, to 678.25 by the midday break. Advancing stocks outpaced losers 669 to 89, with 88 stocks remaining unchanged.

"Investors now have a sort of immunity to the strikes as they have lasted for a long time. Today the crisis was expected to deepen but the reality was different," Park Byung-moon, head of sales at LG Securities, told Reuters.

"Investors think the impact from the strikes has already been reflected on the stock prices. Strikes are more than offset by improving market fundamentals," said a Ssangyong Investment and Securities broker.

South Korea's export-driven industries have been idle since a series of wildcat strikes erupted in protest at the passing of a new labour law on December 26 designed to make the local labour market more flexible.
An across-the-board rebound on Tuesday of blue chips -- most of them export-dependent manufacturers -- showed investor concern over the industrial unrest had diminished.
Chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co rose 3,400 won to 47,400, just off its daily limit high of 47,500.
Hyundai Motor Co, South Korea's largest carmaker and one of the major casualties from the strikes, jumped 6.17 percent (1,400 won) to 24,100 won per share.
Shares of shipbuilding firms were also higher. Daewoo Heavy Industries Co was up 2.12 percent at 5,310 won.

Stocks tumbled about 10 percent at the start of the strikes but regained lost ground early last week, led by financial shares that rose on talks mergers and acquisitions could become active in banks and brokerages.
That speculation was sparked by President Kim Young-sam who said last week a panel would be set up to oversee restructuring of the financial industry. Details have yet to be drawn up.
A slowdown in the economy and an overhang of loans used for margin trading dampened sentiment on South Korean stocks in 1996. The market fell 26.9 percent to end the year at 651.22.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions had called out its 1.2 million members on Tuesday for a two-day strike to try to force the government to dump the new labour law which allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
They were to be joined on Wednesday by members of the 500,000-strong Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has vowed an indefinite walkout against the law.
But buses and subway trains were running almost normally on Tuesday while the number of taxis on the street fell slightly.

Brokers also said signs of improving market fundamentals such as an increase in customer deposits with brokerages had boosted sentiment. Many investors had sold shares in the last six months to pay loans to brokerages falling due.

"It's the first time in three months that customer deposits have outpaced margin loans. This is a really big boost and now supports hopes that the market has taken off for a major rebound," said Park from LG Securities.

Outstanding margin loans have fallen to 2.56 trillion won ($3 billion) from around 2.8 trillion late last year, while customer deposits have steadily grown to 2.58 trillion won from around 2.4 trillion.
